Quintilian, XI.3.71. to make a gesture with head alone, or to make one frequently, was seen as a fault by teachers of drama. To strike one’s forehead in grief seemed the gesture of an orator to Cicero, but to Fabius [Quintilian] that of an actor. But
Cicero, De Oratore III.59.221. in the face and countenance are all things: and in that, all mastery belongs to the eyes. For the countenance is the image of the heart and mind, and it is the eyes that show it.
Ibid., = Orator 18.60, from which the following sentence is also taken. Therefore just as you should make sure that nothing is unsuitable or affected, so there should be great moderation in the expression of the eyes, which have as many forms of meaning and communication as there are emotions of the heart and mind.
Cicero, De Oratore III.59.221. Faults of the nostrils, lips, chin,
The 1618 edition correctly reads ‘menti’ for 1621’s ‘mentis’. neck and shoulders are marked to a higher degree.
Cf. Quintilian, XI.3.80–83, which lists the faults.

Demosthenes would toss his shoulders about: but this fault he is said to have corrected, in this way: that when he spoke standing on a certain narrow platform, a spear would hang down directly over his shoulder, so that if in the heat of speaking he failed to avoid this fault, he would be warned of it by its striking him.
Ibid., XI.3.130.

p.hi: On gesture of the arm, hand and fingers

div.p:
But the arm is extended rather forwards, like a kind of weapon of oratory:
Cicero, De Oratore III.59.220. this is greatly becoming in uninterrupted and flowing passages; and [F2r] when something more beautiful or richer is to be said (such as that passage ‘rocks and desert places reply to the voice’), it is extended wide, and the speech itself spreads out with that military gesture.
In the margin, Quintilian, XI.3 [84, referencing Cicero, Pro Archia 8.19]; ‘that military’ is an addition of Talon’s. And the left arm, if anything is to be done with it, should be raised only so far as to make as it were its normal angle.
Quintilian, XI.3.141. But the hand, though not too lively, and following the words with the fingers, not expressing them,
Cicero, De Oratore III.59.220. has so much power that the action would seem missing without it.
Cf. Quintilian, XI.3.85. For the other parts of the body assist the speaker; but the hand almost speaks itself.
Ibid. Hence those lines of Persius, Satires IV [6–8]:

So when the mob, their indignation roused, is raging,
your spirit brings you the power to make silences of the fiery rabble
by the dignity of your hand-gesture.

But the left hand never makes a gesture by itself; but often matches itself to the right hand.
Ibid., XI.3.114. Thus that aporia of Gracchus’,
See above, chapter 4. ‘Where shall I take myself, wretch that I am?’ should be acted with hands joined. How great a gesture indeed the joining of hands is, an example from the poet [Virgil] shows; Aeneid I [93–6]:

He groaned and holding out both palms to the stars
cried out these words: O thrice and four times blessed
those whose fate it was, in sight of their parents before the high walls of Troy, to die! …

Here the poet shows the gesture first.
Virgil’s word ‘duplices’ [I.93], which I have translated as it is usually taken, ‘both’, could perhaps be taken to mean ‘one over the other’ (cf. Aeneid IX.707), which may be how our author understands it. But to clap the hands is a theatrical gesture.
Quintilian, XI.3.123. And so much for the whole hand: but in its fingers there is a certain particular gesture to each; and above all that most common one, by which the middle finger is joined to the thumb, with three fingers extended,
Ibid., XI.3.92. and this is a rather insistent gesture; and the one with three fingers pressed to the thumb,
Ibid., XI.3.94. and the index (which Antonius indicates that Crassus made skilful use of to express pain of heart and vehemence
Cf. Cicero, De Oratore II.45.188.) is extended. [F2v] This is used in reproaching and pointing out (indicando, hence the name of that finger); with the hand after being held at the shoulder by turns slightly lowered, in affirmation; turned towards the ground, it is insistent; sometimes it is used for the number one.
Quintilian, XI.3.94; modern editions read ‘adlevata’, ‘raised to the shoulder’ rather than ‘by turns’; ‘one’ is added by Butler. Also, very appropriate for modest speech is this gesture, in which the first four fingers come together gently into a point and the hand is brought towards us, either to the face or the chest, and then, facing downwards and stretched out a little, is relaxed.
Ibid., XI.3.96. Quintilian believes that it was in this manner that Demosthenes began that speech on behalf of Ctesiphon with its timid and subdued beginning; and that Cicero’s hand was similarly formed when he said ‘If I have any ability – and, judges, I have a sense of how slight it is’, etc.
Ibid., XI.3.97, quoting Pro Archia 1.1. So remarkable indeed is gesture of the fingers.

p.hi: On gesture of the chest, thigh and foot
For the other parts of the body the faults have chiefly been noted: as, to thrust out the chest and stomach;

note.p: Cf. ibid., XI.3.122.

p.hi: to beat the chest is a theatrical gesture for Fabius [Quintilian].

note.p: Ibid., XI.3.123.

p.hi: But to strike the thigh (which Cleon is believed to have been first to do at Athens) is frequently done, and is both becoming to the indignant, and exciting to the listener.

note.p: Ibid. Modern editions read ‘indignantes’, more idiomatically, for Talon’s ‘indignatos’.

p.hi: And as regards the feet, the stance and the taking of steps is to be observed.

note.p: Ibid., XI.3.124.

p.hi: And to change sides frequently from right to left, putting one’s weight on one foot at a time, is absurd.

note.p: Cf. ibid., XI.3.128, though Quintilian has only ‘indecore’ for Talon’s ‘ridiculum’.

p.hi: However the stamping of the foot at the beginnings and ends of a vigorous argument, is appropriate.

note.p: Ibid., quoting Cicero, De Oratore III.59.220.

p.hi: To take steps is permissible to the orator, but infrequently,

note.p: Cf. Quintilian, XI.3.126 and Orator 18.59.

p.hi: and only in public cases where the stage is large and spacious, and when there are many judges, and hence in the senate, and in an assembly where many are distant.
But it is most unsuitable to run about: and Flavius Virginus wittily asked of the sophist opposing him, how many miles he had declaimed.

note.p: Quintilian, XI.3.126.

div.p:
And
The final paragraph is printed in italic, with the quotation in roman. In 1618 it is the other way round. so much for gesture of the body, which was truly a marvellous instrument of eloquence to the great orators. But indeed against those orators who were scornfully dismissive of this same practice, an argument was taken up. For when Tullius [Cicero] was speaking against [Marcus] Calidius, he put, as an argument of refutation against the charge, that he had conducted the case of poisoning attempted on him so lamely, so calmly, so listlessly, and without gesture of the body. ‘Would you, Marcus Calidius,’ he said, ‘behave so, unless you were making it up? Above all, when you’re in the habit of fending off other men’s dangers so passionately with that eloquence of yours, would you take so little trouble about your own? Where is the pain? Where is the fire in your soul, that usually has the skill to extract speech and grievances even from those who cannot speak? There’s no emotion, no disorder of the body; no striking the forehead, nor the thigh; not even – the least we could expect – a stamp of the foot. As a result so far were you from setting our hearts aflame, we could hardly hold off falling asleep’.
Cicero, Brutus 80.277–8. Thus did Tullius [Cicero] taunt Calidius in the very lawcourts, as if he were a fellow student of his in some college of rhetoric, insufficiently industrious and thoughtful in the discipline that he was professing.
